summary: FIREWATCH is a web application for Indonesia that harmonizes NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections into one consistent dataset. Using NASA FIRMS data, we standardize both sensors' observations, flag candidate corresponding detections by spatial and temporal proximity, and keep unmatched detections, so fires are not double-counted. The dashboard has an interactive hotspot map, a harmonized burning-activity calendar, a MODIS vs. VIIRS vs. harmonized comparison, historical analysis, and anomaly detection that explains why a period was flagged against a statistical baseline. Our web application covers Indonesia (mainly Central Kalimantan) and records from 2022 to 2025. A General View and a Technical View serve both communities and teams such as Satgas Karhutla. Recurring forest and peatland fires in Indonesia harm public health, ecosystems, and livelihoods, and no single sensor shows the full picture. FIREWATCH is a decision-support tool and does not replace field verification.
details:
What it does

FIREWATCH combines MODIS and VIIRS fire detections for Central Kalimantan into a harmonized dataset. It shows that dataset on an interactive map and a daily/monthly/yearly calendar, compares the two sensors, analyzes historical patterns, and flags unusual activity.

How it works

1.      Download MODIS and VIIRS active-fire data from NASA FIRMS.

2.      Clean the data and standardize shared fields (latitude/longitude, date/time, satellite, instrument, confidence, FRP, source dataset).

3.      Match candidate corresponding detections within [1 km and 3 hours]. These are experimental thresholds, and we [tested alternatives: describe the effect on matching].

4.      Keep unmatched detections and assign harmonized observation IDs.

5.      Aggregate daily, monthly, and yearly counts.

6.      Flag anomalies against a statistical baseline (historical averages, standard deviation thresholds, rolling averages) and show the reason for each flag.

7.      Export static JSON for the dashboard.

Benefits

•       Avoids the double-counting (duplication) that comes from simply adding the two sensors' counts.

•       Every anomaly flag comes with an explanation instead of an opaque risk score.

•       General View uses plain language; General/Technical View shows FRP, confidence, matching status, and methodology.

•       Clearly labels satellite detections as observations, not confirmed fires.

What we hope to achieve

To make satellite fire data easier to understand and use for monitoring and field-verification decisions, starting with Central Kalimantan and expandable to other provinces and periods.

Limitations

•       Hotspots are not confirmed ground fires.

•       A candidate match is not proof of the same physical fire.

•       An anomaly is an unusual pattern, not a prediction.

•       Clouds, observation timing, and sensor resolution affect detections.

Tools

Python (Pandas, NumPy, SciPy/Haversine), Leaflet.js, Chart.js, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, JSON, SQL Lite.
